task: Write one sentence of your own using the word oblique. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know oblique should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Tia's oblique postcard said only that the mountains 'ask nothing of anyone,' and the family understood she wasn't coming home soon.
Diplomatic is milder than oblique — the message is softened and cushioned, but it still arrives by the front door.
Veiled goes further than oblique: an oblique remark approaches from the side, while a veiled one hides its meaning almost entirely.

A roundabout answer takes the long way to the point — extra clauses, detours, delay before the meaning arrives. Oblique is about the angle, not the length: a single short oblique line can land its point instantly, just never head-on.

Sidelong is delivered from the side, like a glance you feel rather than meet — it belongs mostly to looks and glances. Oblique reaches further: remarks, criticism, and whole approaches can be oblique, angled away from head-on while still carrying their full message.
aimed straight at the point
open and honest without softening
Oblique is Latin obliquus, 'slanting.' The ob- ('against, aslant') is a familiar prefix, but the -liquus half survives in no other English word, so there is no cousin to peel off.
Oblique means indirect; not straightforward.
The piano teacher never says a performance failed; her oblique verdict — 'the metronome missed you today' — sends students back to the practice room unasked.
Oblique means approaching at a slant instead of head-on: an oblique remark delivers its message while never stating it, leaving the listener to close the last step of the distance.
Oblique praises or accuses indirection, depending on who is speaking — oblique hints, oblique criticism, an oblique approach.
Plain 'indirect' is flatter; oblique adds the sense of an angle chosen on purpose.

Asked directly whether the novel's failed sea captain was based on her father, the author smiled and talked instead about tides.
Her answers all evening were oblique in just that way: never a refusal, never a yes, always a short remark angled off to one side of the question.

Pressed about the book's ending, she said only that 'harbors forgive the ships that miss them.' A less patient interviewer might have called it evasion, but the audience began to hear the answers hiding inside the angles.
By the end, no question had been met head-on, and none, somehow, had gone unanswered.
